plan.title: Electrical Wiring Fundamentals: Circuits & Protection
plan.hook: Every circuit is a bargain between three quantities — pressure, flow, and opposition — and every safety device in a panel exists because one particular way of breaking that bargain hurts people.
objectives: State what voltage, current, and resistance each describe and how Ohm's law relates them
Explain why current needs a closed loop and how series and parallel arrangements share voltage and current differently
Match overcurrent, ground-fault, and arc-fault hazards to the devices that guard against each

sections.heading: Voltage, current, and resistance
sections.body: Voltage is electrical pressure, current is flow of charge, resistance opposes that flow. Ohm’s law relates them.
sections.visual: Current moves through a circuit when a voltage drives it against resistance.

questions.q: What does each of voltage, current, and resistance describe?
questions.hint: The body introduces them as pressure, flow, and opposition — assign each term.
questions.answer: Voltage is electrical pressure, current is the flow of charge, and resistance opposes that flow. Ohm's law relates the three quantities.

questions.q: How does Ohm's law tie the three quantities together?
questions.hint: The diagram writes it as a single equation.
questions.answer: V = I × R: the voltage driving a circuit equals the current multiplied by the resistance it works against.

sections.heading: Complete paths matter
sections.body: Current needs a closed loop. Series and parallel arrangements share voltage and current differently.
sections.visual: A complete path lets charge circulate; an open switch stops the flow.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Complete paths matter"><title>Complete paths matter</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Complete paths matter</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M150 150 L650 150 L650 280 L150 280 Z" fill="none" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="3" class="lw-flow"/><text x="400" y="220" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle">Closed loop</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Open switches interrupt the loop</text></svg>

questions.q: Why does an open switch stop the current everywhere in a simple loop?
questions.hint: What does current require of the path it travels?
questions.answer: Current needs a closed loop. An open switch breaks the loop, so charge cannot circulate and the flow stops.

questions.q: Do series and parallel arrangements treat voltage and current the same way?
questions.hint: The body says the two arrangements share them — but how?
questions.answer: No. Series and parallel arrangements share voltage and current differently, which is why the layout of a circuit matters, not just its parts.

sections.heading: Different hazards need different protection
sections.body: Overcurrent, ground-fault, and arc-fault hazards need different devices. Match the device to the hazard.
sections.visual: Fuses and breakers handle overcurrent; GFCI handles ground faults; AFCI handles dangerous arcs. One device does not cover every hazard.

questions.q: Why is one protective device not enough for a whole panel?
questions.hint: Count the distinct hazards the section names.
questions.answer: Because the hazards are different: overcurrent, ground faults, and arc faults are distinct dangers, and each needs its own kind of device. Protection is hazard-specific, not one-size-fits-all.

questions.q: Which device handles a ground fault, and which handles overcurrent?
questions.hint: The diagram pairs each hazard with its device.
questions.answer: A GFCI handles ground faults. Fuses and breakers handle overcurrent. Dangerous arcs are the AFCI's job.

questions.q: In the language of this course, resistance is…
choices: What opposes the flow of charge
questions.explain: Voltage is the electrical pressure and current is the flow of charge. Resistance opposes that flow, and Ohm's law — V = I × R — relates all three.

questions.q: A voltage drives current through a circuit. What does the current have to work against?
choices: Nothing — voltage alone sets the flow
questions.explain: Current moves through a circuit when a voltage drives it against resistance. That opposition is exactly what resistance names.

questions.q: A lamp in a simple loop goes dark the moment a switch opens, even though the switch is on the far side of the loop. Why?
choices: Current needs a closed loop, and the open switch breaks it
The voltage drops to zero at the power source
Charge drains out through the open switch
questions.explain: Current needs a closed loop to circulate. An open switch interrupts the loop anywhere, so flow stops throughout it.

questions.q: Series and parallel circuits differ in that they…
questions.explain: The body states it directly: series and parallel arrangements share voltage and current differently. The quantities and their units are the same in both.

questions.q: A breaker keeps tripping on an overloaded circuit, but a damaged cord is leaking current to ground without overloading anything. Which device addresses the second hazard?
questions.explain: Fuses and breakers handle overcurrent — the first hazard. The GFCI is the device matched to ground faults; match the device to the hazard.

questions.q: Why does the course insist that protection is "hazard-specific, not one-size-fits-all"?
choices: Because panels are too small for multiple devices
Because overcurrent, ground-fault, and arc-fault hazards are different dangers needing different devices
Because each device only works at one voltage
Because fuses and breakers are being phased out
questions.explain: The three hazards are distinct: overcurrent is handled by fuses and breakers, ground faults by a GFCI, and dangerous arcs by an AFCI. No single device covers every hazard.

sections.title: Pressure, flow, and opposition
bullets: Current is the flow of charge.
Ohm's law links them: V = I × R.
sections.notes: Keep the three roles separate: voltage pushes, current flows, resistance pushes back. Ohm's law is the equation that ties the three together.
sections.visual: Current moves through a circuit when a voltage drives it against resistance.

sections.title: No loop, no current
bullets: Current needs a closed loop to circulate.
An open switch interrupts the loop and stops the flow.
Series and parallel arrangements share voltage and current differently.
sections.notes: A circuit is a loop, not a line. Break it anywhere — one open switch is enough — and charge stops circulating everywhere. How components are arranged then decides how voltage and current are shared.
sections.visual: A complete path lets charge circulate; an open switch stops the flow.

sections.title: Match the device to the hazard
bullets: One device does not cover every hazard.
sections.notes: Each protective device exists for a specific failure. Overloading, leaking to ground, and dangerous arcing are three different hazards, so the panel carries three different answers.
sections.visual: Fuses and breakers handle overcurrent; GFCI handles ground faults; AFCI handles dangerous arcs. One device does not cover every hazard.

enrichment.audioTitle: Electrical Wiring Fundamentals: Circuits & Protection — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Start with three words: voltage, current, resistance. Give me a one-line job description for each.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Voltage is pressure, current is the flow of charge, and resistance... is how much wire there is?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Close — resistance opposes the flow. Voltage drives current against that opposition, and Ohm's law ties them together: V = I × R.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: So if I know any two, the third follows.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That is the point of the law. Next: a switch opens on the far side of a loop and the lamp next to the battery dies too. Why?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Because the current was used up before reaching the switch?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Current is not used up — it needs a closed loop to circulate. Open the loop anywhere and the flow stops everywhere.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: And whether parts are in series or parallel changes how they share voltage and current.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Right. Now protection. A breaker handles overloads. A cord is leaking current to ground but drawing normal current. Is the breaker the right guard?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: It would not trip — there is no overcurrent. That hazard needs a different device.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: A GFCI, for ground faults. And arcs get an AFCI.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly: fuses and breakers for overcurrent, GFCI for ground faults, AFCI for dangerous arcs. Why not build one device that does all three?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Because the hazards themselves are different — protection is hazard-specific, not one-size-fits-all.
